small_guidance:
- Add larger BLOCK_SP configs (512) and try BLOCK_OC tiling smaller than full OC (e.g. 32) to reduce register pressure on the (BLOCK_OC, BLOCK_SP) accumulator — but for min-reduction across all OC you need full OC; consider a two-stage: tile OC and reduce min across tiles via atomic-min or a second pass. Sweep num_warps in {4,8,16}.
- The current x gather is non-coalesced because IC=16 is laid as the K-dim (rows of the x tile) — load shape is (IC, BLOCK_SP) with IC strided by 1 in NHWC; transpose tile layout so BLOCK_SP is contiguous along the IC axis (use x_tile of shape (BLOCK_SP, IC) and tl.dot(x_tile, w_tile.T)) so the inner loads are fully coalesced across SP.
- Cache reused ih/iw input rows across kw inner loop by hoisting kh loop outside and reusing the loaded x for overlapping ow positions; or pre-load a (BLOCK_SP, IC) tile per (kh,kw) once. Also try `tl.multiple_of`/`tl.max_contiguous` hints on sp_offs to enable wider vector loads.
large_guidance:
- Restructure as an implicit-GEMM where each program computes a tile of (BLOCK_SP) output pixels for a single n, accumulating across the K=IC*KH*KW dim with BLOCK_K loop, holding ALL OC in registers (OC=64 fits) so the channel-min can be done in-register before store. Use NHWC input with BLOCK_SP contiguous and weight laid out as (K, OC) so the GEMM is x[BLOCK_SP, BLOCK_K] @ w[BLOCK_K, OC]; min over OC then double-tanh fused at epilogue. This makes input loads fully coalesced and weight loads broadcast-friendly.
- Alternatively, since OC=64 and IC*KH*KW=144 are tiny, try a persistent kernel with one program per (n, sp_tile) that streams the 144-element K-loop with vectorized loads of 4 IC at a time (IC=16 → 4 chunks of 4) and uses tl.dot on (BLOCK_SP, 4) x (4, OC) micro-tiles — this trades dot size for better L1 reuse of weights (weights fit in ~36KB, fully cacheable).
- Consider fusing the NCHW→NHWC permute into the kernel by indexing the original NCHW tensor directly (compute n,c,ih,iw offsets inside), eliminating the contiguous() copy that currently runs before the kernel and likely accounts for a meaningful fraction of the 3.08ms.
